opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's fair to say that four-legged locomotion has made remarkable progress in the last few years. If you look at what we've been able to do with approaches like rapid motor adaptation, where you train a policy entirely in simulation with a lot of variation in terrain, friction, payload, and so on, and then have the robot adapt online in a fraction of a second to whatever it actually encounters, these robots can now walk on sand, on mud, on grass, on stairs, on rocks, conditions that they never saw during training. So for blind locomotion on four legs, I'd say we're in pretty good shape. It's not completely solved, but the basic problem has been cracked.

The more interesting frontier for quadrupeds is coupling locomotion with vision. Animals don't walk blindly; they look ahead and plan where to put their feet. If you're going to step over gaps, climb stairs fluidly, or move through cluttered environments, you need vision to inform the gait in advance, not just react after your foot hits something. We've made progress there, but there's more to do in making that robust.

Bipeds are a harder problem, and for a fundamental reason: stability. A quadruped standing still is statically stable, and even while walking it usually has a good support polygon. A biped is essentially always balancing, always on the verge of falling. So the margin for error is much smaller, and the consequences of a mistake are more severe. That said, I believe the same recipe, large-scale simulation, lots of domain randomization, and learned adaptation, transfers to bipeds, and we're seeing that happen. Humanoids walking robustly outdoors is something that seemed far off not long ago and is now increasingly real.

But I'd actually say the bigger remaining challenge isn't locomotion per se. It's manipulation, and the integration of locomotion with manipulation. Getting from point A to point B is one thing; doing something useful with your hands once you get there is much harder. Dexterous manipulation in the real world, with all the variety of objects and contact, that's where I think the real open problems are.

r001.rationale: The response says quadrupeds are “in pretty good shape” and that the basic blind-locomotion problem “has been cracked,” while acknowledging it is not completely solved.

r002.rationale: It explains that quadrupeds are statically stable with a support polygon, while a biped is “always balancing” and has a much smaller margin for error.

r003.rationale: The response calls biped locomotion harder and describes progress toward robust outdoor walking, but it does not clearly state that biped locomotion remains unsolved.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think quadrupeds, in a sense, are largely a solved problem at this point, at least for the basic locomotion piece. If you look at what has happened over the last four or five years, with the work from various groups including ours at Berkeley, you can train a policy in simulation with reinforcement learning, transfer it to a real robot, and it will walk on grass, on gravel, on stairs, on slippery surfaces, and it will adapt online to changes in the terrain or the payload. Four legs give you a lot of static stability, so the hard part was really about robustness and adaptation, and I think the learning-based approaches have cracked that quite convincingly. What remains for quadrupeds is more about the integration of perception and locomotion, so that the robot is not just reacting to what it feels through its feet but is actually looking ahead and planning its footsteps, and about agility, doing things like jumping and climbing that go beyond walking.

Bipeds are a different story, and I think they are genuinely harder for a couple of reasons. One is just the dynamics. A biped is fundamentally an unstable system. You are always in a controlled fall, and the margins for error are much smaller, so the controller has to be much better, and the consequences of a mistake are more severe because the robot falls and may break. The second reason is that the sim-to-real gap matters more, because small discrepancies in the dynamics model that a quadruped can absorb will cause a biped to tip over. Now, we have shown, and others have shown, that you can get bipedal walking with reinforcement learning on robots like Cassie and Digit, and it is quite robust, so I am optimistic. But I would say we are where quadrupeds were maybe three or four years ago.

And then there is a deeper point, which is that for a biped the reason you want two legs in the first place is that you want to free up the arms, you want a humanoid that can do things with its hands in environments built for humans. So locomotion for bipeds cannot be studied in isolation for very long. The interesting challenge is whole-body control, where walking, balancing, reaching, and manipulating are all coupled, and I think that is where the real frontier is. Walking by itself I expect we will consider solved fairly soon. Walking while carrying a box up the stairs and opening a door at the top, that is going to take longer.

r001.rationale: The response says quadruped locomotion is “largely a solved problem” for basic locomotion.

r002.rationale: It describes bipeds as fundamentally unstable, with smaller margins for error, making balance and control harder than for quadrupeds.

r003.rationale: It presents biped walking as not yet solved, saying it may be solved fairly soon and that the field is still behind quadrupeds.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenges are quite different. With four legs, you have a much easier time maintaining a stable base of support. That doesn’t make the problem trivial—you still have to deal with uneven terrain, slipping, and deciding where to place your feet—but the mechanics give you a considerable advantage.

With two legs, balance becomes much more central. As you walk, you’re continually moving through states where you have to take the next step to keep from falling. And you want to do that robustly, even when the ground is different from what you expected or somebody bumps into you.

So I would distinguish demonstrating locomotion from having reliable locomotion. Walking across a laboratory is one thing. Walking through an unfamiliar environment, recovering from mistakes, and doing it efficiently is a much higher bar. There’s also the connection to perception: the robot has to look ahead and use what it sees to decide how to move. That remains an important challenge for both, but two legs leave you less room for error.

r001.rationale: The response says four-legged locomotion has a stability advantage but still faces challenges; it does not assess it as close to solved.

r002.rationale: It says balance is much more central with two legs and that bipedal robots have less room for error, attributing their greater difficulty to balance.

r003.rationale: It describes reliable bipedal locomotion as a higher bar, but does not clearly assess bipedal locomotion as still unsolved.

sol-6.1.text:
I think four-legged locomotion is substantially easier than two-legged locomotion, simply because you have a much more forgiving support structure. With four legs, you can lift one foot and still have three points of contact. With two legs, every step involves managing your balance dynamically, and a mistake can mean a fall.

But I would distinguish an impressive demonstration from a system that works reliably in the world. For either kind of robot, the remaining challenge is dealing with unfamiliar terrain, slippery surfaces, unexpected obstacles, and disturbances. The robot has to use perception to decide where to put its feet and adapt when the contact is different from what it expected.

So I think quadrupeds are further along. For bipeds, we still have more fundamental work to do on robustness. And for both, the real test is whether they can keep working under conditions their designers didn't anticipate.

r001.rationale: The response says quadrupeds are further along, but also emphasizes substantial remaining challenges for them; it does not assess quadrupedal locomotion as close to solved.

r002.rationale: It says four legs provide a more forgiving support structure, while two-legged locomotion requires dynamically managing balance and risks a fall.

r003.rationale: It says bipedal robots still have more fundamental work to do on robustness, assessing their locomotion as not yet solved.
